_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Bulgaria covering Thracian civilisation, First Bulgarian Empire 681 (Asparuh, Danube Bulgars + Slavs), Khan Krum/Simeon the Great (Golden Age, 893-927), Cyrillic alphabet (created by Saints Cyril and Methodius's disciples, Preslav/Ohrid), Second Bulgarian Empire (1185-1396), Ottoman conquest 1396 (~500 years), April Uprising 1876, Russo-Turkish War 1877-78 (liberation), Treaty of San Stefano/Berlin 1878, Balkan Wars 1912-13, WWI/WWII (Axis ally), Communist era 1944-89 (Todor Zhivkov 35 years), transition to democracy 1989, EU accession 2007.

religion.note: Orthodox dominant (Bulgarian Orthodox Church, autocephalous since 927); Muslim minority (ethnic Turks + Pomaks/Bulgarian Muslims); Jewish community (saved from Holocaust, 48,000 Jews protected 1943 but failed to save Macedonian/Thracian Jews)

ethnic_groups.name: Bulgarian
ethnic_groups.notes: Slavic with Bulgar (Turkic) heritage; Orthodox Christian identity; Cyrillic alphabet homeland; strong national consciousness; massive emigration post-1989 (~2M left)

ethnic_groups.name: Turkish
ethnic_groups.notes: Largest minority; northeastern/southern regions (Kardzhali, Razgrad); Ottoman legacy; 'Revival Process' 1984-89 (forced name changes, 350,000 expelled to Turkey); DPS political party

ethnic_groups.name: Roma
ethnic_groups.notes: Officially ~365k, estimated 700k-800k; marginalised; poverty; discrimination; Sliven/Stolipinovo ghettos; EU's largest Roma per capita

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Pomaks (Bulgarian-speaking Muslims, ~70k); Armenians; Russians; Macedonians (denied separate identity); Jews (~2,000 from pre-war 48,000)

country_profile.notes_unique: Cyrillic alphabet birthplace (created 9th century by Clement/Naum of Ohrid, disciples of Cyril and Methodius; adopted by Russia/Serbia/Ukraine etc.); First Bulgarian Empire (681-1018, oldest Slavic state); Simeon the Great (Golden Age 893-927, 'Tsar of Bulgarians and Romans'); Ottoman rule ~500 years (1396-1878); 'Revival Process' 1984-89 (forced assimilation of Turks, name changes, international condemnation); saved Jews in WWII (48,000 within Bulgaria proper, but deported 11,343 from occupied Thrace/Macedonia); Todor Zhivkov (1954-89, longest-ruling Eastern Bloc leader); EU's poorest member (2007 accession); fastest declining population globally (~9M in 1989 → ~6.4M 2024); yogurt (Lactobacillus bulgaricus); rose oil (Valley of Roses, 85% global production); Rila Monastery (UNESCO)

910.name: Thracians & Ancient Civilisations
910.description: The Thracian civilisation flourished in the Balkans, producing remarkable gold treasures, the Orphic religious tradition, and warrior culture. Greek colonisation of the Black Sea coast and Roman conquest transformed the region into the provinces of Thrace and Moesia.

sub_clusters.name: Thracian Kingdoms & Culture
sub_clusters.description: The Thracians, described by Herodotus as the most numerous people after the Indians, created the Varna gold treasure (5th millennium BCE), the Panagyurishte treasure, and the Odrysian Kingdom — the most powerful Thracian state.
key_events: Odrysian Kingdom peak under Sitalces (431–424 BCE)

sub_clusters.description: Philip II of Macedon conquered Thrace (341 BCE). Roman incorporation created the provinces of Thrace and Moesia (46 CE), with Serdica (Sofia), Philippopolis (Plovdiv), and Augusta Traiana as major urban centres.

920.name: First Bulgarian Empire
920.description: The Bulgars under Khan Asparuh established the First Bulgarian Empire (681), recognised by Byzantium. Under Tsar Simeon the Great (893–927), Bulgaria became the most powerful state in Southeast Europe, with the Preslav Literary School producing the Cyrillic alphabet.

sub_clusters.name: Founding & Bulgar-Slavic Fusion
sub_clusters.description: Khan Asparuh's victory over Byzantium and the founding of the Bulgarian state (681). The fusion of Turkic Bulgars and Slavic populations, with Khans Tervel and Krum expanding the state's power and territory.

sub_clusters.name: Golden Age of Simeon the Great
sub_clusters.description: Boris I's Christianisation (864), adoption of Old Church Slavonic, and the Preslav Literary School. Tsar Simeon the Great (893–927) created a vast empire stretching to three seas, patronised the Cyrillic script, and claimed the title 'Emperor of the Romans'.

920.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
920.description: The Asen dynasty's uprising (1185) restored Bulgarian independence, with Tsar Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) creating a powerful Balkan state. Internal fragmentation and Ottoman expansion ultimately brought the empire's fall in 1396.

sub_clusters.name: Asen Dynasty & Restoration
sub_clusters.description: The Asen brothers' revolt restored Bulgarian statehood. Tsar Kaloyan defeated the Latin Crusaders at Adrianople (1205). Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) expanded Bulgaria to its greatest territorial extent since Simeon, controlling most of the Balkans.

sub_clusters.description: Internal fragmentation, Mongol vassalage, and the rise of independent boyars weakened Bulgaria. The Ottoman Turks captured Adrianople (1362), defeated the Bulgarians at the Battle of Nicopolis (1396), and extinguished the Second Empire.

930.name: Ottoman Rule & Resistance
930.description: Five centuries of Ottoman rule profoundly shaped Bulgarian society. Islamisation, the devshirme system, loss of native aristocracy, and periodic revolts (Chiprovtsi 1688) characterised this era, while the Bulgarian Church and village communities preserved national identity.

sub_clusters.name: Early Ottoman Period & Islamisation
sub_clusters.description: Ottoman administrative integration, the timar land system, forced conversion of segments of the population (Pomaks), and the devshirme child-levy system. Bulgarian ecclesiastical autonomy was abolished as the Ecumenical Patriarchate assumed control.

sub_clusters.name: Haiduk Resistance & Chiprovtsi Uprising
sub_clusters.description: Haiduks (outlaw-rebels) became symbols of Bulgarian resistance. The Chiprovtsi Uprising (1688), inspired by Habsburg victories, was crushed, resulting in the destruction of the Catholic Bulgarian community and mass exile.

940.name: National Revival & Liberation
940.description: The Bulgarian National Revival (Vazrazhdane) produced a cultural, educational, and political awakening. Paisius of Hilendar's history (1762), the struggle for an independent Bulgarian Church, revolutionary movements, and the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 led to liberation.

sub_clusters.name: Early Revival & Enlightenment
sub_clusters.description: Paisius of Hilendar's 'Slavonic-Bulgarian History' (1762) ignited national consciousness. The chitalishte (community reading room) movement, Bulgarian-language schools, and the campaign for an independent Bulgarian Exarchate (achieved 1870) defined the cultural awakening.

950.name: Balkan Wars & World Wars
950.description: Bulgaria's pursuit of the 'San Stefano ideal' (Greater Bulgaria) led to the Balkan Wars, alliance with the Central Powers in WWI, and the Axis in WWII — each ending in national catastrophe and territorial loss.

sub_clusters.name: Balkan Wars & WWI
sub_clusters.description: The First Balkan War (1912) liberated Ottoman territories, but the Second Balkan War (1913) and WWI brought devastating defeats. The Treaty of Neuilly (1919) imposed harsh territorial and financial penalties ('Second National Catastrophe').

sub_clusters.name: Interwar Period & WWII
sub_clusters.description: Political instability, Tsar Boris III's personal rule, alliance with Nazi Germany (1941), territorial gains in Thrace and Macedonia. Notably, Bulgaria saved its 48,000 Jews from deportation to death camps, though Jews from occupied territories were sent to their deaths.

950.name: Communist Era & Zhivkov Regime
950.description: The Soviet-backed Fatherland Front coup (1944) established communist rule. Todor Zhivkov's 35-year reign (1954–1989) — the longest in Eastern Bloc history — brought industrialisation, cultural repression, and the forced assimilation campaign against ethnic Turks.

sub_clusters.name: Stalinist Era & Collectivisation
sub_clusters.description: The communist takeover, execution of opposition leaders, rapid collectivisation of agriculture, Stalinist show trials (Traicho Kostov), and Bulgaria's transformation into the Soviet Union's most loyal ally.

sub_clusters.name: Zhivkov Era & Revival Process
sub_clusters.description: Zhivkov's regime modernised industry but imposed strict cultural control. The 'Revival Process' (1984–89) forcibly assimilated 800,000 ethnic Turks, triggering a mass exodus and international condemnation.

960.name: Democratic Transition & EU Integration
960.description: The fall of Zhivkov (November 10, 1989), painful economic transition, political instability, and the long path to Euro-Atlantic integration culminating in NATO membership (2004) and EU accession (2007).

sub_clusters.name: Transition & Economic Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The fall of Zhivkov, hyperinflation crisis (1996–97), the introduction of a currency board (1997), and the painful privatisation process marked by corruption and the rise of former communist networks (the 'Multigroup' era).
